      <title>Serial pulse oximetry measurements in primary care to improve triage and referral decisions for children</title>
      <scientificTitle>Serial oximetry for improved triage and referral of children presenting to primary care</scientificTitle>
      <acronym>SOfTeR</acronym>
      <studyHypothesis>The aim of the “Serial Oximetry for Improved Triage and Referral” (SOfTeR) study is to improve care and management of children with hypoxaemia who present to primary care facilities in Nigeria and Malawi.  This aim will be addressed through answering these specific research questions:
1.	What proportion of children who present to outpatient settings with an SpO2 <95% return to a normal oxygen saturation SpO2 95-100%) within 1-hour?
2.	What demographic and clinical factors identify children who present with an SpO2 <95% that returns to normal within 1-hour and within 3-hours? 
3.	How can triage and referral pathways be adapted to safely manage children in primary care settings who present with an SpO2 <95%?
4.	Is a prolonged period of SpO2 observation for children in LMIC outpatient settings acceptable to healthcare workers and caregivers?</studyHypothesis>
      <plainEnglishSummary>Background and study aims
To improve child survival, the World Health Organisations Integrated Management of Childhood Illnesses guidelines need to balance inpatient treatment of higher risk moderately hypoxaemic children, whilst not overwhelming the health system with unnecessary referrals of children from primary care. This study will establish how often hypoxaemia spontaneously resolves and describe factors that lead to either spuriously low SpO2 measurements or temporary desaturation that can be managed in outpatient settings. Ultimately, this will facilitate more specific guidelines that minimise burdens associated with referrals and preserve resources within the healthcare system without compromising on access to oxygen for those in need. The aim of the “Serial Oximetry for Improved Triage and Referral” (SOfTeR) study is to improve care and management of children with hypoxaemia who present to primary care facilities in Nigeria and Malawi. This aim will be addressed through answering these specific research questions:
1.	What proportion of children who present to outpatient settings with an SpO2 <95% return to a normal oxygen saturation (SpO2 95-100%) within 1 hour?
2.	What demographic and clinical factors identify children who present with an SpO2 <95% that returns to normal within 1-hour and within 3-hours? 
3.	How can triage and referral pathways be adapted to safely manage children in primary care settings who present with an SpO2 <95%?
4.	Is a prolonged period of SpO2 monitoring for children in LMIC outpatient settings acceptable to healthcare workers and caregivers?

Who can participate?
The study will involve two types of participants, children and wider healthcare stakeholders. Children will be eligible if they are ≥2 months to <10 years, present to primary care with an acute condition, and have an SpO2<95% as measured by study staff. For wider stakeholders will include caregivers of recruited children, healthcare workers from study facilities, practitioners and implementers, and decision makers, including facility managers, district/LGA or State level decision makers. 

What does the study involve?
We will conduct three sub-studies: a) a prospective cohort of children with severe and moderate hypoxaemia who present to primary care facilities; b) a quality-of-care assessment for medical oxygen at the referral facility; c) a qualitative study of the acceptability and potential design of different triage approaches for primary care. 

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There are three potential risks for participants, but overall, this should be outweighed by the potential benefit to children and healthcare systems. The first is the conduct of malaria and haemoglobin testing, that requires an invasive blood prick. Malaria RDTs are commonly conducted in both settings, and we estimate that up to 50% of children would have this done as part of routine care (when tests are available). For these children, the study would not pose any additional pain or distress than could be expected as part of standard care. The second risk is the duration of the observation period within primary care, as we will ask caregivers and their child to remain for 1-3hours. We will not stop any child from being immediately referred, but are aware that even in cases of referrals, children can stay at the facility for over an hour. The final is the  time-burden on clinical and facility staff, and the risk of taking them away from clinical tasks. To mitigate this we will plan the data collection for a time that is convenient, and will allow for returning visits. 

Where is the study run from?
The study will be conducted in Sweden, Malawi and Nigeria, as a research collaboration between Karolinska Institutet Sweden, Oxygen for Life Initiative Nigeria and Centre for Research and Development Institute Malawi.  

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
Recruitment for the study is expected to start in March 2027, and finish by December 2029. 

Who is funding the study?
The Swedish Research Council (reference: 2025-02236)

Who is the main contact?
Prof Carina King (carina.king@ki.se, ck2031@bath.ac.uk)</plainEnglishSummary>

    <interventions>
      <intervention>
	<description>We will conduct two sub-studies: a) a prospective cohort of children with severe and moderate hypoxaemia who present to primary care facilities; b) a qualitative study of the acceptability and potential design of different triage approaches for primary care. 

a) A prospective cohort of children aged ≥2 months to ≤10 years old, presenting to primary care outpatient settings with an oxygen saturation <95% will be followed to determine if their SpO2 returns to normal (i.e. 95-100%) and how long that takes. Recruited children will be monitored by study staff within facilities for 1-3 hours and then followed-up at 3-days and 14-days to ascertain onward care and survival. The purpose of this cohort is to try and understand which children were incorrectly classified as being hypoxaemic, which children had transient hypoxaemia, and which have persistent of worsening SpO2 values and  need  referral and hospitalisation. 

b) We will use multiple qualitative methods to understand whether a prolonged triage approach or alternative monitoring and referral patient pathways are acceptable, feasible to implement and desirable for healthcare workers, caregivers and wider stakeholders. We will start with stakeholder mapping and consultations, to understand how the process of guideline modifications and revisions are done in each country, and who is involved in the process. This serves multiple purposes: to ensure the right people are invited to co-design, to generate buy-in for the idea of differentiated care pathways, and to provide legitimacy when we discuss with healthcare workers and caregivers. We will then conduct in-depth interviews with caregivers and focus group discussions (FGDs) with healthcare workers, that will inform (alongside findings from sub-study 1), a co-design workshop with key stakeholders in oxygen systems and child health in Nigeria and Malawi.</description>

      <title>Choice of anti-malarial drugs for chemoprevention</title>
      <scientificTitle>Drug choice for malaria chemoprevention: comparison of hydroxychloroquine or amodiaquine with or without sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine in Malawi - a factorial, individually randomised, double blind, placebo controlled trial</scientificTitle>
      <acronym>CHAMP Drug</acronym>
      <studyHypothesis>Primary objectives:
Randomisation 1 : To evaluate the effect of amodiaquine and hydroxychloroquine each compared to placebo on the prevention of hospitalization due to malaria during the intervention period (day 0-150). 
Randomisation 1 : To evaluate the effect of amodiaquine and hydroxychloroquine each compared to placebo on the incidence of uncomplicated clinical malaria in children under five years of age during the intervention period (day 0-150). 
 
Randomisation 2 : To evaluate the efficacy of SP versus placebo on the prevention of uncomplicated clinical malaria during the intervention period (day 0-150). 
 
Secondary objectives:
Randomisation 1: Comparison of hydroxychloroquine or amodiaquine versus placebo
1.1 To evaluate the effect of hydroxychloroquine or amodiaquine, compared with placebo, on all-cause hospital admission during the intervention period (days 0-150)
1.2 To evaluate the effect of hydroxychloroquine or amodiaquine, compared with placebo, on all-cause mortality during the intervention period (days 0-150)
1.3 To evaluate the effect of hydroxychloroquine or amodiaquine, compared with placebo, on the incidence of severe malaria, as defined by WHO criteria, during the intervention period (days 0-150)
1.4 To assess the impact of hydroxychloroquine or amodiaquine, compared with placebo, on malaria transmission potential, using gametocytaemia as a proxy indicator, during the intervention period (days 0-150)
1.5 To assess the impact of hydroxychloroquine or amodiaquine, compared with placebo, on the number of hospitalisation events due to malaria during the post-intervention period (days 150-365)
1.6 To assess the impact of hydroxychloroquine or amodiaquine, compared with placebo, on the number of uncomplicated clinical malaria events, defined as RDT positive with fever or a history of fever, during the post-intervention period (days 150-365)

Randomisation 2: Comparison of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine versus placebo
2.1 To evaluate the effect of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, compared with placebo, on non-malaria outcomes, including:
2.1.1 All-cause hospital admission during the intervention period (days 0-150) and the post-intervention period (days 150-365)
2.1.2 All-cause mortality during the intervention period (days 0-150) and the post-intervention period (days 150-365)
2.1.3 Number of infections requiring antibacterial or antimalarial treatment during the intervention period (days 0-150)
2.1.4 Change in haemoglobin concentration during the intervention period (days 0-150)
2.1.5 Changes in weight, height, and weight-for-height z-scores during the intervention period (days 0-150)

These apply to both randomizations:
3.1 To characterise the pharmacometric relationship between antimalarial drug exposure, including parent drug and relevant metabolites, and prevention of blood-stage infection
3.2 To assess the safety and tolerability of chemoprevention regimens during the intervention period (days 0-150)
3.3 To investigate the relationship between molecular markers of antimalarial drug resistance and the efficacy of chemoprevention regimens</studyHypothesis>
      <plainEnglishSummary>Background and study aims
Malaria is a major health problem in Malawi and other parts of sub-Saharan Africa. Children under 5 years of age are especially at risk of becoming seriously ill or dying from the disease. Medicines can be given regularly to prevent malaria, but it is not yet clear which drugs work best in East and Southern Africa, where patterns of malaria transmission and drug resistance differ from other regions.

This study aims to find out whether three antimalarial medicines, hydroxychloroquine, amodiaquine and sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, can safely and effectively prevent malaria in young children. The researchers will compare these medicines with placebo (dummy treatment) and assess whether they reduce malaria illness, malaria-related hospital admissions, and other health problems. The results will help guide future malaria prevention policies in Malawi and similar countries.

Who can participate?
Children aged 3 months to 59 months can take part if they:
• Live in the study area and are expected to remain there during the study period
• Have a parent or guardian who gives consent for participation
• Have a parent or guardian willing to follow the study requirements, including attending a designated health centre if the child develops malaria symptoms

Some children cannot participate, including those with known allergies to the study medicines, certain medical conditions, or specific medicines that could interact with the study treatments.

What does the study involve?
The study plans to enrol about 6,900 children in Mwanza District, Malawi.

Participants will be randomly assigned to receive one of several combinations of study medicines or matching placebos. Neither the families nor the study team will know which treatment a child receives during the study.

The study medicines will be taken by mouth once each month for 5 months. Some medicines will be given for 3 consecutive days each month, while others will be given as a single dose.

Children will attend scheduled study visits where researchers will monitor their health, record any illnesses, and measure growth. Blood samples will be collected to test for malaria infection, measure haemoglobin levels, assess drug levels in the body, and study markers of malaria drug resistance.

Researchers will follow participants during the treatment period and for several months afterwards to record malaria episodes, hospital admissions, and other health outcomes.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
Children taking part may benefit from protection against malaria, although this cannot be guaranteed. Participants will receive regular health assessments, and any illnesses identified during the study can be assessed by the study team.

As with any medicine, there is a risk of side effects. Some children may experience adverse reactions to the study drugs, although participants will be monitored closely for safety throughout the study. There may also be some discomfort from blood sample collection.

The information gained from the study could help improve malaria prevention for children in Malawi and other countries in the future.

Where is the study run from?
The study is run by the Malawi Liverpool Wellcome Programme and the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine.
Study activities will take place in Mwanza District, Malawi, including Mwanza District Hospital, Kunenekude Health Centre, Thambani Health Centre, and Tulonkhondo Health Centre.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
The study is expected to begin enrolling participants in October 2026. Recruitment is planned to continue until November 2026. The overall study is expected to run until December 2027.

Who is funding the study?
The study is funded by the GiveWell Community Foundation, United States of America.

Who is the main contact?
Dr Donnie Mategula
donnie.mategula@lstmed.ac.uk</plainEnglishSummary>

    <interventions>
      <intervention>
	<description>This is a factorial, individually randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with six treatment arms arising from two independent randomisations administered concurrently. All study drugs are given orally at monthly intervals for five months (~days 0, 30, 60, 90, and 120).

Randomisation 1 allocates participants in a 1:1:1 ratio to:
- Hydroxychloroquine: 154 mg base per day (children aged over 12 months) or 77 mg base per day (children aged under 12 months) for 3 consecutive days per monthly cycle
- Amodiaquine: 153 mg base per day (children aged over 12 months) or 76.5 mg base per day (children aged under 12 months) for 3 consecutive days per monthly cycle
- Matching placebo: identical in appearance to active drug, for 3 consecutive days per monthly cycle

Randomisation 2 allocates participants within each Randomisation 1 arm in a 1:1 ratio to:
- Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP): 500 mg/25 mg (children aged over 12 months) or 250 mg/12.5 mg (children aged under 12 months) as a single dose per monthly cycle
- Matching placebo: single dose per monthly cycle

This produces six treatment combinations: HCQ+SP, HCQ+placebo, AQ+SP, AQ+placebo, placebo+SP, and double placebo.</description>

    <results>
      <ipdSharingStatement>The datasets generated during and/or analysed during the current study will be deposited in a controlled-access repository following completion of the study. Details of the specific repository will be confirmed and updated at a later date.

Type of data: Pseudonymised individual participant data (IPD) including clinical outcomes (malaria-related hospitalisation, clinical malaria episodes, adverse events), laboratory results (blood slides, filter paper analyses, plasma), sociodemographic data, drug exposure measures, and molecular markers of antimalarial resistance. Direct identifiers (name, date of birth, household GPS coordinates, and mobile phone numbers) are stored separately from analysis datasets and will not be shared.

When available and for how long: Pseudonymised datasets will be made available following publication of the primary trial results. Data will remain available for the duration of the study's 25-year retention period, in accordance with clinical trial regulatory requirements.

Access criteria and with whom: Data will be shared with qualified researchers who submit a scientifically sound research proposal, subject to approval by the study team and relevant ethics and data governance bodies. Access will be governed through the repository's access management system and formal data-sharing agreements.
Types of analyses: Secondary analyses consistent with the study objectives, including epidemiological analyses, drug efficacy modelling, resistance marker analyses, and health outcomes research.

Mechanism: Researchers will submit access requests through the designated repository platform. Approved requestors will receive pseudonymised datasets under a signed data-sharing agreement specifying permitted uses, security obligations, and conditions of publication.

Consent: Written informed consent will be obtained from the caregiver of each participant prior to enrolment. Participants will be  informed of the possibility of pseudonymised data being shared with collaborating institutions for approved research purposes.

Data anonymisation: All datasets for sharing will be pseudonymised prior to transfer, with direct identifiers removed and stored separately under restricted access at MLW. Re-identification is not possible without the linking code held securely at MLW.

Ethical and legal restrictions: Data sharing is subject to compliance with Malawi National Health Sciences Research Committee ethical approval and relevant data protection regulations, including those applicable to LSTM as joint data controller. Shared data may not be used for purposes beyond those specified in the approved data-sharing agreement.

Other comments: Data will be collected using ODK eCRFs on secure encrypted Android tablets, transmitted to the MLW ODK Central server, and protected by multi-layered access controls at device, form, and server levels. Biological samples transferred to MORU/University of Oxford for approved analyses are governed by a material transfer and data-sharing agreement between the institutions.</ipdSharingStatement>
